description: A large, dark bear, moving slowly through the underbrush with a quiet, deliberate grace. It knows you are here. It does not care.
A small, round bear cub, no bigger than a dog, with soft fur. It watches you with open curiosity and absolutely no fear.
A mother bear, large and watchful, with a single small cub trailing close behind. She has one ear tilted toward the cub at all times.
A mother bear with two cubs, both tumbling over each other as they follow her. She walks slowly, letting them keep up.
A mother bear with three cubs, all climbing over the same fallen log in different directions. She waits, patient, at the far end.
Two bear cubs wrestling in a patch of soft moss, growling at each other in tiny, serious voices. Their mother is somewhere close, watching.
A tall buck, antlers broad and crown-like, standing perfectly still at the edge of a clearing. He has heard you, but he has not decided what you are.
A quiet doe, grazing with her head low, one ear turned toward the woods. She is beautiful and unremarkable, in the way that all wild things are.
A small, spotted fawn, standing alone in the tall grass, perfectly still. It believes, with all its heart, that if it does not move, you cannot see it.
A doe and her single fawn, walking together down a shaded trail. The fawn stays so close that its nose touches her flank.
A doe with twin fawns, one on each side, all three stepping in perfect unison. It looks like a small parade.
A small herd of deer, moving through the trees as one silent shape. A dozen sets of dark eyes catch the light at once, then vanish.
A male fox, sleek and red, sitting on a fallen log with his tail curled around his paws. He watches you with one eye and pretends to sleep with the other.
A vixen, smaller and sharper than the dog, moving through the ferns with her nose to the ground. She is hunting, and she is not being quiet about it.
A single fox kit, all ears and mischief, chasing its own tail in a patch of sunlight. It stops the moment it sees you, then resumes.
A vixen with a single kit, watching it pounce on a dry leaf with great seriousness. She is proud of it, obviously.
A vixen with two kits, each one trying to steal the other's stick. She pretends not to notice.
A vixen with three kits, all of them rolling in the dirt. She looks tired, and she looks happy. Both can be true.
A large, calm buck rabbit, sitting perfectly still in the shade of a fern. He has decided you are not a threat. He is watching to be sure.
A quiet doe rabbit, nibbling clover with tiny, delicate bites. Her ears turn toward you before her eyes do.
A single rabbit kit, small enough to fit in your palm, blinking up at you from a nest of dry grass. It has not yet learned to be afraid.
A doe rabbit with several kits, all huddled together in a shallow nest. She watches you from a few feet away, tense and ready.
A scatter of rabbits across a meadow, all grazing separately and all somehow aware of each other. If one bolts, they all will.
A grey squirrel, sitting on a low branch with its tail curled over its head like an umbrella. It chatters at you with clear disapproval.
Two squirrels, one chasing the other around and around a trunk. Neither seems to know who is chasing whom.
A mother squirrel, with two tiny pink babies clinging to her belly. She moves carefully, aware of her passengers.
A single chipmunk, sitting bolt upright on a stone, cheeks bulging with something it refuses to share. It is impossible to take seriously.
Two chipmunks chasing each other through the leaf litter, stopping every few seconds to stare at you, then resuming.
A single field mouse, sitting on a fallen leaf, washing its face with tiny, careful paws. It has not noticed you.
A small family of mice, all huddled together under a curl of bark. There are four of them, and they are all breathing in unison.
A small, round vole, sitting still in a patch of grass, watching the sky. It looks very thoughtful for a creature with so little to think about.
A tiny shrew, all nose and appetite, darting through the leaf litter. It has already eaten three times today and is hungry again.
A mole, dark and velvety, surfacing briefly from its tunnel to push up a small mound of fresh soil. It is gone again before you can blink.
A stocky badger, moving slowly through the underbrush with the unhurried confidence of an animal that has never been in a hurry in its life.
A badger mother, walking with a single small cub at her side. She is teaching it to sniff for roots. It is teaching itself to be distracted.
A single otter, lying on its back in the grass beside a stream, cracking a mussel open on a stone balanced on its chest. It looks up, unbothered.
Two otters, sliding down the same muddy bank again and again, chittering with obvious delight. They have been at this for an hour.
A family of otters, parents and pups, swimming in a slow line across the pond. The smallest pup rides on its mother's back.
A weasel, long and sinuous, slipping out of one burrow and into the next. It pauses, mid-glide, to look at you with bright, curious eyes.
A mink, dark and sleek, moving along the streambed with the easy confidence of an animal who owns the water and knows it.
A striped skunk, ambling across the clearing without a care in the world. It has no reason to hurry, and it knows it.
A skunk mother with two small kits, both following her in a neat, waddling line. She glances back at them every few steps.
A porcupine, sitting high in a tree and staring out at nothing in particular. It is in no hurry. It has never been in a hurry.
A mother porcupine, moving slowly along a branch, with a single small porcupette following behind. The baby is very careful about where it puts its feet.
A raccoon, sitting on a fallen log and washing a piece of food in a puddle with great concentration. It looks up, and does not seem embarrassed.
A raccoon mother with three kits, all of them trying to climb the same tree at once. She watches from the base, patient as stone.
An opossum, hanging upside down from a low branch by its tail, staring at you with dull surprise. It does not seem sure what is happening.
A mother opossum, walking slowly along the ground with a cluster of tiny babies clinging to her back. There are seven of them. She is very tired.
A groundhog, sitting up on its haunches in the middle of a clearing, watching you with open suspicion. It has been watching you since you entered the meadow.
A beaver, working on a dam with quiet, focused attention. It has been at this for months. It will be at it for months more.
Two beavers, one on land and one in the water, sharing a single branch between them. They work in silence, side by side.
A beaver family, parents and kits, all working on a lodge in the fading light. The kits mostly play. The parents mostly rebuild what the kits have torn down.
A massive bull moose, standing in the shallows of a pond, chewing thoughtfully on a lily pad. He is the largest thing you have ever seen up close.
A cow moose, with a single long-legged calf at her side, wading through the marsh. The calf is all knees and uncertainty.
A bull elk, standing alone in a clearing, his antlers catching the low sun. He is bugling. The sound fills the entire valley.
A herd of cow elk, grazing in a meadow, all facing the same direction. They move as one, without any apparent signal.
A lone wolf, silver and grey, standing on a ridge and watching you with calm, patient eyes. It has been here longer than you have.
A pair of wolves, one grey and one black, walking side by side along a game trail. They are not hunting you. They want you to know that.
A small pack of wolves, four or five of them, crossing a clearing in a loose, quiet line. The largest is in front, but it is not the leader.
A pair of coyotes, one singing from a rise and the other answering from a hollow. Their voices are close enough to be having a conversation.
A small pack of coyotes, yipping together in a wild, chaotic chorus. It sounds like a party. It is a hunt.
A bobcat, sitting on a rock in the sun, tail flicking idly. It has seen you. It does not care. It has decided you are not worth the effort.
A bobcat mother, walking with a single kitten at her side, its tufted ears enormous on its small head. It is trying very hard to look serious.
A lynx, pale and ghostly, slipping through the trees like a thought. You see it for a second. You may never see it again.
A single garter snake, basking on a warm stone, coiled into a neat spiral. It watches you with one bright, unblinking eye.
A tiny, dark snake, no longer than your hand, slipping through the grass. It has more important things to do than meet you.
A single green frog, sitting on a lily pad in a small pond, its throat pulsing gently. It is watching a fly. It is not watching you.
A chorus of frogs, calling together from every direction at once. You cannot see a single one, but the air is full of them.
A single brown toad, sitting in a patch of dirt at the base of a tree, blinking slowly. It has the calm of something very old.
A spotted salamander, moving through the damp leaves with slow, deliberate steps. It is beautiful and utterly unbothered by you.
A box turtle, walking slowly across a clearing, its shell shining with rain. It has been walking since before you arrived. It will still be walking long after.
A small, brown lizard, sitting on a sun-warmed stone, doing tiny push-ups. It is either exercising or threatening you. It is hard to tell.
A tangled patch of blackberry brambles, thorns crossing every which way. There are berries deep inside, but they are not going to be easy to get to.
A patch of bracken ferns, waist-high, their fronds curling at the tips. Beneath them, the light turns green and soft.
A gorse bush, dense and prickly, covered in bright yellow flowers that smell faintly of coconut. Do not try to walk through it.
A low patch of purple heather, spreading across the ground like a soft rug. It hums with bees, though you cannot see them.
A young hazel sapling, its long catkins swinging in the breeze. It is trying very hard to look like a real tree. It is not quite there yet.
A young hawthorn, all thorns and no blossoms yet. It is already defensive. It will grow into its beauty, but it will keep the thorns.
A wild rose scrub, sprawling low across the ground, its canes tangling into the ferns. It has one small, perfect pink blossom, and a hundred thorns.
A tangle of wild raspberry canes, arching over each other. They are covered in tiny thorns and, deeper in, a handful of red berries.
A young holly, glossy and sharp, growing low in the shade. Its berries are still green, and the branches are already hostile.
A scrubby elderberry bush, short and crooked, with a few small white flowers just coming in. It is not much to look at. It will be glorious in a month.
A small spicebush, leaves faintly aromatic. If you crush one between your fingers, the whole world smells like allspice for a moment.
A young witch hazel, its leaves still small and unassuming. In a few months, it will bloom in yellow and surprise everyone.
A cinnamon fern, tall and elegant, its spore stalks standing up like small brown spears. It is one of the oldest plants in this forest.
A lady fern, delicate and lacy, growing in the deep shade of a boulder. Its fronds move in the smallest breeze.
A royal fern, majestic and tall, growing in a damp hollow. It looks like it has been here since the beginning.
A maidenhair fern, fine and black-stemmed, clinging to a mossy ledge. Each frond is a small green fan.
A patch of stinging nettles, tall and dark green. Beautiful. Dangerous. Do not touch.
A cluster of tall thistles, crowned with purple blossoms and defended by spines. The bees love them. Your fingers will not.
A stand of fireweed, tall and pink, growing where the ground was disturbed. It is the first flower to return to a broken place.
A low patch of wood sorrel, its tiny, heart-shaped leaves folding shut at the first touch. It tastes faintly of green apples.
A patch of wild strawberries, tiny and bright red, hidden in the grass. There are not many. Each one is worth the search.
A patch of wild garlic, its leaves broad and bright green, the whole clearing smelling faintly of onion when the wind moves through.
A tall stand of reeds, growing thick at the edge of a small pond. They sway together, making a soft, papery sound.
A cluster of cattails, their brown heads bursting with soft seed. If you touch one, the whole head comes apart in your hand.
A stand of bulrushes, tall and straight, leaning slightly in the wind. They look like they are listening to something.
A soft, rounded hummock of moss, growing over an old stump. It is the perfect size to sit on, and the perfect softness to fall asleep on.
A patch of liverwort, flat and green and strange, growing over a rock like a living map. It has no roots. It drinks the air.
A carpet of clubmoss, tiny and evergreen, spreading across the forest floor. It looks like a miniature forest in its own right.
A fallen log, half-sunk into the earth, its bark soft and alive with moss. It is slowly becoming soil.
A fallen log with a hollow along its length, worn down by years of water and weather. It is a highway for the smallest creatures.
A rotting stump, crumbling at the top, ringed by young ferns. It is full of life and returning to the earth, one year at a time.
A large boulder, coated in a thick layer of moss. It has been here longer than the trees around it, and it will be here after they are gone.
A boulder split clean down the middle, with a small maple seedling growing from the crack. Nature is patient and stubborn in equal measure.
A patch of small, smooth pebbles, left behind by a stream that has long since changed course. They are warm from the sun.
A small patch of pale sand, soft underfoot, piled up in a hollow. It is where a doe beds down at night.
A small, dark puddle, ringed with tiny hoofprints. Deer and rabbits drink here, and the raccoons wash their food here, and the whole forest uses it.
A thick pile of dry leaves, banked up against the base of a tree. It rustles, even when nothing moves.
A small cache of acorns, tucked into a hollow at the base of a tree. A squirrel has been here. The squirrel will return.
A pile of pinecones, stripped clean, at the base of a pine. Squirrels have been at work. They left a mess.
A large fallen branch, broken off in a storm, still green in places. It will not last the winter.
A scatter of small, wild apples, fallen and softening in the grass. Wasps are busy. Deer will come at dusk.
A young tree, torn from the ground and left to die, its roots drying in the air. It is a sad thing to see.
A tangle of roots, exposed where the soil has washed away, snaking across the ground. There is a small hollow beneath them, just big enough to hide in.
A warren of rabbit burrows, openings scattered across a low bank, connected by a maze of tunnels. Rabbits have lived here for generations.
A fox den, worn into the base of a bank, smelling faintly of musk and old leaves. A vixen has raised several litters here.
A badger sett, dug deep into a hillside, with several entrances and a worn patch of earth out front where the badgers like to sun themselves.
A beaver lodge, domed and sturdy, built of sticks and mud. It is warm inside, even in the coldest part of winter.
A beaver dam, blocking a small stream and turning it into a quiet pond. It is a masterpiece of engineering and stubbornness.
An otter holt, tucked under the roots of a riverside tree, with a worn path leading down to the water. The otters have been here for years.
A shallow ground nest, lined with grass and a few soft feathers, holding three speckled eggs. The mother is watching from somewhere. She is watching you.
A shallow hollow in the dirt where birds have been rolling, leaving a dusting of fine earth. It is a spa for sparrows.
A mud wallow, churned and dark, with deer tracks in every direction. It smells of wet earth and animals.
A tree with the bark rubbed raw at shoulder height, the wood beneath polished smooth. Something large has been scratching here for years.
A small, dark scent mark on a low branch, left by a fox or coyote. It is a signpost. The forest is full of them.
A single shed antler, white and clean, lying in the grass. A buck left it here last winter. It is warm from the sun.
A long, translucent snakeskin, caught on a low branch and trailing down. It is dry and papery and completely empty.
A scatter of small feathers, brown and grey, on the ground. There was a struggle here. Or a molt. It is hard to say.
A cluster of broken eggshell fragments, pale blue and speckled, scattered in the grass. Something hatched here, or something was eaten.
A small pile of clean bones — a rib, a vertebra, a small skull — bleached white and half-buried in the leaves. An owl has been feeding here.
A pile of owl pellets, dry and grey, packed with fur and tiny bones. The owl itself is somewhere above, asleep in a tree.
A small pile of deer droppings, dark and round, fresh and glossy. A deer passed this way recently, and not in a hurry.
A scatter of rabbit pellets, small and round and dark, in a neat patch of grass. They are not as unpleasant as they sound.
A single tapered dropping, dark and twisted, left deliberately on a stone. Foxes mark their territory like this.
A small tuft of grey fur, caught on a low branch. Something passed through here and left a piece of itself behind.
A set of clear deer tracks, pressed into the soft mud beside a stream. Two of them, walking slowly, side by side.
A set of tiny, hand-like tracks, pressed into the mud. A raccoon has been here, washing something in the stream.
A single, enormous paw print, pressed deep into the mud. Five toes, long claws, and a shape you will not forget.
A delicate scatter of three-toed bird tracks, pressed into the mud. Something small and quick has been here, hunting for insects.
A small stack of flat stones, balanced carefully one on top of another. Someone built this. Someone will build another.
A tree with a small, old blaze cut into its bark — a mark from a trail long since abandoned. Someone wanted to remember the way.
A narrow, worn path, pressed into the forest floor by generations of hooves. It leads somewhere. It always leads somewhere.
Four deep claw marks, scored into the bark of a tree at shoulder height. A bear stood here, and stretched, and marked the tree as its own.
A young tree, its bark rubbed smooth and bare from years of deer and elk rubbing against it. It has been loved to death.
An old den, long abandoned, half-collapsed and filled with leaves. Something lived here once. It has moved on.
A small burrow, tucked under a fallen log, just big enough for a mouse or a chipmunk. There are seeds scattered at the entrance.
An old stump, hollowed out by rot, now a perfect, dark hiding place. The inside is lined with soft moss.
A tumble of old stones, half-buried in the earth, all that remains of a wall someone built long ago. Now it is just a place for moss and mice.
A ring of stones around a patch of blackened earth, cold for many seasons. Someone sat here once, and looked up at the same sky.
A patch of black earth and charcoal, where a fire burned hot and long. Nothing grows here yet.
A single, smooth glowstone, resting in the moss at the edge of a clearing. It glows softly, pink and warm. Birds are fond of them, but they like to keep the pink ones and often drop them here.
A small cluster of glowstones, nestled together in a hollow between roots. Each glows a different color, and their lights mingle into a soft, quiet rainbow.
A single fern whose fronds glow faintly with a soft, green light. It grows only in the deepest shade, where the sun never quite reaches.
A patch of soft moss that whispers back whatever you say to it, in a voice so quiet you almost think you imagined it.
A single reed, growing at the edge of a pond, that hums a low, steady note when the wind moves through it. It is always in tune.
A small, still pool, reflecting the sky so perfectly that it is hard to tell where the water ends and the sky begins. At night, it shines silver.
A cluster of tiny, glowing motes, drifting together in the air above a patch of moss. They move as one, as if following music you cannot hear.
A smooth, grey stone, cool to the touch, with a faint spiral etched into its surface. If you hold it and make a wish, it grows warm for just a moment.
A thick root, exposed where the soil has washed away, that shows a single, silent image of the forest's past when you touch it. Then the image fades, and it is just a root again.
A small, pale mushroom that repeats the last sound it heard, over and over, until the sound fades into nothing.
A single flower, dark purple, that grows only in deep shadow and closes the moment any light touches it.
A single, pale petal that glows faintly at dawn and grows cool and dim by midday. It is impossible to pick. It falls apart in your fingers.
A single firefly that glows steadily, without flickering, and seems to follow you as you walk. It never lands. It never leaves.
A small butterfly with wings that shimmer faintly, like a piece of the night sky. It moves slowly, and where it lands, the ground glows for a moment.
A small, clear stream that burbles and giggles over the stones, as if it finds something endlessly funny. It is impossible not to smile.
A small, flat stone with a hole worn through it. When the wind passes through the hole, it hums a low, steady note. It sounds like the earth remembering.
A small stone carved with a single rune, its lines glowing faintly. The rune is old, older than the forest, and it spells a word no one remembers how to speak.
A small, pale flower that glows only when you are asleep. If you wake in the night and look, it will be shining. If you watch it, it will not.
A small, moss-covered stone figure, worn almost beyond recognition, at the base of an old tree. Someone carved it long ago. Someone still leaves flowers.
A perfect circle of pale mushrooms, growing in a clearing, glowing faintly in the dusk. If you step inside, the air smells of honey. If you step out, it does not.
A narrow trail of glowing moss, winding between the trees, leading somewhere you cannot quite see. It is only visible at dusk.
A single moonpetal, silver-white, growing at the edge of a shadow. It will open at dusk and close at dawn. It will never open in daylight.
A small fragment of dark bark, covered in slow-moving stars, resting on a bed of moss. It is cold to the touch, and warm to hold.
A small, smooth pebble that quietly repeats your last word back to you, in your own voice, a second after you say it.
A single, pale acorn, warm to the touch, humming a soft, wordless tune. It stops when you move away. It starts again when you return.
A single root, glowing faintly like a banked ember, warm but never burning. It lights the soil around it in soft, orange hues.
A single, frozen dewdrop that never melts, resting on a blade of grass. It hums a tiny, high note when touched.
A small stone with a hollow inside it, big enough to hold a single drop of water. If you speak into it, your voice comes back older.
A small, folded note, tucked into the moss at the base of an old tree. It reads: 'If you have walked this far, you are almost home. Whoever you are, I am glad you came.'
